rv.q: Steven Levenson’s script is unflaggingly wily and kicks off from a very intriguing premise.

Yet if the prospect of spending an evening contemplating the perils of peer pressure, family breakdown and rampant social media seems less than inviting, be reassured that Dear Evan Hansen is worth it.
It’s tender and timely and affectionately funny.
If you’re the one waving through a window, it’s Dear Evan Hansen that’s waving back.
At the same time, the evening does feel – much like its protagonist – supremely calculated; and for all its cleverness, there is an air of chilliness about it.

It looks so simple but there’s something incredibly accomplished about the way that ‘Dear Evan Hansen’ fleshes out its lovable protagonist’s small world of home, school and laptop – then creates a trap that feeds him and poisons him all at once.
Until the soppy perfunctory ending – with hugs and instructions about being true to yourself – the evening is vivid with almost every kind of teenage and adult embarrassment and exclusion.
The music and lyrics by Benj Pasek and Justin Paul – who collaborated on the movies La La Land and The Greatest Showman – are good enough to overcome the occasional holes in the story.
But as one of their paymaster parents, I found myself more appreciative than excited.
Alas, my own eyes stayed as dry as Prince Andrew’s armpits.
Ultimately, this is a high school drama about stalkers, trolls and those who piggyback on tragedy.
It’s a heartfelt show whose originality is its trump card.
To find out, you will have to go and see the best musical to have been written in the last ten years.
The result is something quite extraordinary – a musical not like any other.
This fantastic show is selling out fast and rightly so.
“Ghost Quartet” casts its own singular, truly vital spell.
Move over, Ben Platt - we've found our own Evan Hansen, and he's the real deal.
For the most part, this is a musical with real emotional heft, its raw, confessional songs going for the jugular – leaving audience members openly weeping.
As such, it could not be more welcome.
Steven Levenson's gripping story is unlike any of the many US high school shows you've ever seen.
The result is moving but never melodramatic or preachy.
Or, to put it bluntly, it’s good but samey.

cn.t: Critics praise this Tony-winning musical for tackling teen suicide and social media with sophistication and a standout performance from Sam Tutty, though some find it overhyped. The bold subject matter and catchy Pasek/Paul score earn widespread admiration.
